newsitem.title: INDIA: India relieved but wary as political crisis eases.
newsitem.headline: India relieved but wary as political crisis eases.

text.p: Indians breathed a sigh of relief on Wednesday at the end of a 24-day political crisis, but questions lingered over why it had happened and whether it would occur again soon.
Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral won a vote of confidence in parliament late on Tuesday, pulling the curtain down on a period of upheaval that Hindu nationalists called unnecessary.
The tame parliamentary debate and Gujral's easy victory after more than three weeks of political fury gave way to public relief that the confusion was over.
"I am relieved because the uncertainty has ended," said M.L. Seghal, owner of a general store in the capital.

But like many other citizens on the street as well as commentators in the press, Seghal was sceptical. "Gujral is a good and honest man with experience. But the other parties are not good. Within a year he will be brought down," he said.

The minor changes in government seemed out of proportion to the depth of the crisis, which nearly poisoned ties between the governing United Front coalition and its indispensable ally, the Congress party, and took the nation to the brink of snap polls.
Congress's surprise decision on March 30 to revoke its support for the 10-month-old United Front government was the death knell for prime minister H.D. Deve Gowda's leadership.
Deve Gowda lost a vote of confidence on April 11. After vowing to stick by its leader, the United Front eventually bowed to Congress pressure and replaced Deve Gowda with Gujral.
But in a telling sign of continuity, Gujral, 77, reappointed all but five of Deve Gowda's ministers to his own cabinet and was trying to persuade four of the others to come back.
Opposition leader Atal Bihari Vajpayee of the Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) called the turmoil needless and Congress's move an irresponsible act.
"Why was Deve Gowda singled out and why did the country need a new prime minister?" Vajpayee asked parliamentarians.

Congress party president Sitaram Kesri had already acknowledged his motives stemmed largely from his troubles with Deve Gowda, accused of trying to split India's oldest party and embroil its leaders in criminal cases.
"The party of 140 MPs needs respect and attention," Congress whip Santosh Mohan Dev said. "Do not treat us as your doormat."
Gujral, who was said to be on good personal terms with Kesri, promised a different approach. "There will be no witch hunting," Gujral told the lower house of parliament.
That comment provoked Vajpayee, who said Gujral had revealed the real reason for Deve Gowda's fall related to scandals touching both Congress and the coalition.

The murky nature of the crisis prompted much scepticism about Kesri's motives and Gujral's future. "The entire issue got reduced to the change of leadership in the United Front," columnist Kuldip Nayar wrote in the Hindustan Times.
"Has anybody calculated the loss to the nation, which has 300 million people living below the poverty line?" he said, noting the government had been paralysed for almost a month.

"This crisis will never be over," said Amarjeet Singh, who owns an import-export company in Delhi. "Yesterday it was Deve Gowda. Today it is I.K. Gujral. Tomorrow Kesri will stand up and change I.K. Gujral again."
Rahul, an iron manufacturer from the northern city of Chandigarh, said: "Definitely Kesri will repeat it after some time. Then this chap Gujral will be toppled."
